title_en: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy criticises Trump for calling Putin his ‘friend’; Kyiv deploys new laser weapon
excerpt_en: Ukrainian leader likens Putin to Hitler; laser system intercepts Russian drone but not ready for ‘mass deployment’. What we know on day 1,739
body_en: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has criticised Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin his “friend”, likening the Russian leader to Adolf Hitler. “Of course it’s up to the president of the United States, but... it’s strange,” the Ukrainian leader told the BBC in an interview aired on Friday. “He is an aggressor, and a killer... He can’t be a friend. Just cannot be. It’s the same that somebody says about Hitler during the second world war, that he’s a good friend. No. He’s not a friend.” Zelenskyy said what was needed was “more progress” and urged Washington to increase pressure on Moscow.

Ukraine has for the first time used a laser weapon to shoot down a Russian jet-powered drone, according to its state-backed defence group Brave1. An adviser to Zelenskyy, Serhiy Beskrestnov, published footage earlier this week showing a target crashing in a fireball, saying a Russian Geran jet drone had been shot down by a laser system for the “first time”. Agence France-Presse quoted Brave1 as saying on Friday: “Footage recently emerged online showing a Ukrainian laser system being used in combat to intercept an enemy jet-powered drone.” The weapon was developed by a recipient of a Brave1 grant and operated by a private air defence team, Brave1 added. But it cautioned that “a first successful interception does not mean the technology is ready for mass deployment”. “Laser air defence remains an experimental technology,” it said, adding that at least seven teams in Ukraine were currently working on laser weapons. Beskrestnov said the system, known as Blysk and developed by the Ukrainian company Carmine Sky, was protecting critical infrastructure during the interception.

A convoy of Russian ships carrying military vehicles bound for Libya has turned around in the Mediterranean after Ukrainian maritime drones sank ⁠a Russian naval warship in Benghazi ⁠port last Sunday, Reuters quoted three people from military and security services as saying on Friday. The convoy, which was escorted by the Russian navy frigate Golovko, turned around near the strait of Sicily on the same day as ⁠the attack in Benghazi, said a European military official who had been tracking the convoy. A Ukrainian military intelligence official and a Middle East security official confirmed the flotilla had turned from heading to Libya. Russia’s defence ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Ukraine has offered ⁠a Black Sea ceasefire to enable food ⁠exports and ⁠passed this on to international allies, the foreign minister ⁠said. “We are ready for ⁠a ceasefire. We are grateful to ‌India, Turkey and ‌Egypt, which are playing ‌an active and important role in de-escalating tensions in the Black Sea, as well as in mediation efforts. ‌We are now awaiting a response from Russia,” Andrii Sybiha was cited by public broadcaster Suspilne as saying on Friday. He added that Russia had proposed ⁠Ukraine suspend attacks on the Russian oil sector under the truce, but Kyiv ‌would only consider this as part of a bigger energy ceasefire deal.

Ukraine’s military said on ⁠Friday it ⁠had struck a Russian solid ⁠rocket fuel production site ⁠in the Tula ‌region south ‌of Moscow ‌overnight. “The plant is the starting point of the ‌missile production chain: it manufactures components for plastic explosives and ⁠the polymer used to produce solid propellant for Russian ‌ballistic missiles,” the defence ministry said on Telegram.

Russia’s foreign ministry has accused ⁠Latvia of creating artificial ⁠obstacles ⁠to hinder the transit of Russian grain to ⁠global markets, saying the restrictions pose additional risks ⁠to global food security. Ministry spokesperson ‌Maria Zakharova ‌claimed in a statement published ‌on the ministry’s website on Friday that Latvia was conducting inspections of Russian grain shipments for allegedly ‌stolen Ukrainian agricultural products and was seeking ways to ban Russian grain transit altogether.

title_en: David Jones owed $250m to Chanel, Calvin Klein and others when it collapsed. What comes next?
excerpt_en: What does the department store’s CEO think went wrong – and what is happening to its staff?
body_en: David Jones owed more than $250m to Chanel, Disney and other top companies when it collapsed into administration, on top of other debts, its directors believed.

A new company report also shows customers have raced to spend $15m worth of gift cards in three weeks and provides the most detailed estimate yet of how much David Jones owed its many creditors and suppliers.
The struggling department store chain’s chief executive, in her first public appearance since the collapse, has also warned more job losses and store closures could be announced as buyers circle.
Related: David Jones’ future looks grim. Is Myer next?
So how much did David Jones owe – and what comes next?

Which businesses did David Jones owe money to? The company’s administrator on Thursday filed a report as of 5 November, when it took over. It contains David Jones’s directors’ estimates of the company’s assets and debts at that point.
The directors estimated David Jones owed $164m to regular suppliers. Less than 60 businesses accounted for $100m of that figure, with the biggest debts owed to big name brands
PVH Brands Australia, the subsidiary of the owner of Calvin Klein and Tommy Hilfiger, was owed $11m, followed by Estee Lauder at $7m, L’Oreal at $6.6m and Chanel at $5.7m.
Kim Kardashian’s underwear brand, Skims, cookware company Le Creuset and skincare brand Dermalogica were each owed more than $1m.
Many suppliers had much smaller debts, with Balenciaga owed just $695 and Cotton On owed $49.
Another $52m was owed to suppliers with in-store concession booths, including Country Road ($4m), Louis Vuitton ($3m) and Saba ($1.7m).

Interactive David Jones also owed $26m to service providers, including $2.8m to Telstra, $1.5m to maintenance company ARA Indigenous Services, $1.4m to Origin Energy, $1.4m to Australia Post and $1m to Qantas.

It owed $33,000 to Walt Disney Australia. The department chain has regularly partnered with the entertainment behemoth, with promotions on its Sydney flagship store’s top floor and shop windows featuring Winnie the Pooh.
The company also owed $9.5m in unpaid rent to landlords, $4.5m of which is owed to its main landlord, Westfield’s owner Scentre Group.
How much money did David Jones have? The report for David Jones Pty Limited, just one of the companies in the retailer’s group, also showed the company had an estimated $637m worth of total assets.
Directors believed it had $47m of funds in reserve. It also had $268m worth of stock in inventory that it hoped to sell.

Its property and equipment and shares in subsidiary companies accounted for most of the rest. It was owed about $520m by its related companies including its owners, but also owed related companies $496m.

David Jones also had $46m worth of gift card balances outstanding on 5 November, the report showed. Administrators reported that had fallen to $33m by 17 November and kept falling, meaning customers have spent more than a third of their gift card balances.
What does the CEO think went wrong? Erica Berchtold joined David Jones in mid-2025 and became its chief executive in June.
She could see pressures on the business immediately, with some stores losing millions of dollars a year, she said on 2GB radio on Thursday in her first interview since the collapse.
“Was it the internet? Was it overseas competition? I think it was a bit of a perfect storm of everything,” she said.
“I think we kind of thought that if we were a slightly better version of another department store then that was good enough, and actually it’s not.”

title_en: The Com: the global cybercrime network posing a ‘chilling threat’ to children
excerpt_en: FBI estimates thousands of people identify as members or recent members of group linked to indecent images of girls and blackmail
body_en: It sounds benign: the Com, short for the Community. But crime agencies around the world warn that it is far from that and the young cybercriminals involved are causing havoc and putting children at chilling, sickening risk.

Beau-Jack Mensforth was jailed by a UK judge on Friday for his activities as part of the Com. He was one individual operating from his bedroom in north-east England, but there are probably thousands more like him and parents are being urged by police to be aware and to check their children’s devices.
Related: Man jailed in Newcastle for blackmailing vulnerable girls online

The Com, crime agencies say, is a sprawling and fluid global network of online communities populated by young cybercriminals. A typical Com member is a boy or young man aged 16 to 25. They are primarily native English speakers. Their crimes are broad and may include data theft, crypto scams, bringing down IT systems and causing chaos through attacks that slow down networks.
Then there are young men such as Mensforth who targeted vulnerable young girls and encouraged them to harm themselves or sacrifice their pets.
Often the criminals coerce girls to take indecent images of themselves which they then share. They blackmail and threaten their victims with swatting and doxing, police say.

Swatting is the term used for reporting fictitious incidents at the victim’s address to the emergency services, so they turn up in numbers, sometimes armed. Doxing is threatening to put all of someone’s personal details online.

They operate on every platform, according to DCI Steve Brown of Northumbria police, who led the investigation into Mensforth. “They target people they know have vulnerabilities, people who need somebody to make them feel wanted, to feel valued,” said Brown. “They gain that trust and then they turn that trust against them by asking them to perform horrendous acts.”
In July 2025, the FBI issued its first big public alert about the Com under the headline: “Theft, extortion and violence are a rising threat to youth online”.

The FBI said the Com was a growing and evolving online threat, calling it “a primarily English-speaking, international, online ecosystem comprised of multiple interconnected networks whose members, many of whom are minors, engage in a variety of criminal violations”.
It added: “The FBI estimates thousands of individuals identify as current or recent members of the Com with varying levels of associated activity.”

The UK’s National Crime Agency has said reports of Com networks increased sixfold in the UK from 2022-2024, describing members as “usually young men who are motivated by status, power, control, misogyny, sexual gratification, or an obsession with extreme or violent material”.

The Molly Rose Foundation, a leading UK online safety charity, this year issued a stark public warning about the Com and called for a coordinated global response from governments, regulators, law enforcement and tech companies.

Andy Burrows, the charity’s chief executive, said: “The growing threat posed by Com networks is the most chilling and urgent threat to children online today and it requires a swift and comprehensive response.”
The motivations of Com members vary but, according to the FBI, often fall into one of these categories: “Financial gain, retaliation, ideology, sexual gratification and notoriety.”
They wanted to have control, said Brown. They got a kick out of getting people to do things they would never normally do.
Related: Hot fridges, a fake nuclear alert and a $6bn heist: are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic?

Courts around the world are increasingly dealing with criminals linked to the Com. Sentences vary but there’s thought to be none longer than the 77-year jail term handed down in August, in Tennessee, to Kyle Spitze, 27, for abetting the distribution of animal crushing videos and child sexual exploitation material offences.
The US Department of Justice said Spitze’s crimes occurred as part of his association with an online network known for its “sadistic extortion of young and vulnerable people around the world”.
Crime agencies such as the FBI urge people “to exercise caution when posting or messaging personal information, photos or videos on social media, dating sites or other online platforms”.
For parents it can be bewildering and scary but they do need to monitor their child’s online activity, police say.

After the gruelling slog of the Mensforth case, Brown said he now checked the devices of his own children. “Personally, since this investigation, I do that to my kids,” he said. “It’s simply asking parents: talk, know and act. Talk to your children, know what they’re doing and act upon it.”

title_en: Astronomers ‘disheartened’ by decision allowing SpaceX to deploy satellites for space datacenters
excerpt_en: American Astronomical Society warned that satellites could disrupt research, while others raised concerns about orbital debris and environmental risks
body_en: Astronomers are pushing back against Elon Musk’s Starmind program to place a huge number of AI computers in space, which was given the green light to proceed by federal communications regulators earlier this week.

The American Astronomical Society said it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the decision by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) decision to grant SpaceX a license to deploy as many as 1m satellites in low Earth orbit as a way of moving datacenters into space.

The society said the proposed satellite constellation “would significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky”.

The American Astronomical Society has previously raised concerns about the cumulative impact of reflective, bright satellites on astronomy, both optical and infrared, as well as potentially harmful radio frequency interference affecting radio astronomy.

In addition, it said, “atmospheric pollution from the launches and reentries of so many satellites, as well as increased collision risks in orbit, remain significant concerns; both of these factors threaten research astronomy.”
US federal regulators approved a constellation of satellites to process data in space on Wednesday, saying that they would “support America’s booming super intelligence economy”.
The FCC said in a statement that regulators had approved 1m Starmind orbital satellites, or compute modules, built by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
They said that the authorization “promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization – one that can harness the full power of the sun”.
“America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence,” said the FCC chair, Brendan Carr.
Proponents of the plan argue that datacenters in space are necessary to offset the electricity and water demands of Earth-based AI computing.

SpaceX argued in its submission to the FCC: “By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial datacenters.”

A report published by the government accountability office (GAO) in July said that space-based datacenters “could reduce the land, electricity, and water needed for data centers on Earth” but warned of “engineering and economic barriers to deployment”.

The GAO said datacenters generate excess heat, but space does not cool computing hardware efficiently and “could be a major engineering challenge”. Further, it said, “a significant increase in the number of satellites in orbit could be difficult to manage and cause collisions.”

Under the license approved on Wednesday, SpaceX must begin deployment no later than November 2033, deploy 10% of ⁠the maximum number – or 100,000 – no later than November 2035 and deploy 50% by November 2038, the FCC said.

Approximately 17,000 ‌satellites currently exist, but there are rising concerns about the amount of space debris in higher orbits. The FCC deferred SpaceX’s request to dispose of satellites located above 600km in space “graveyard” orbits.
Amazon’s rival satellite unit, Leo, and others have criticized ⁠the plan, suggesting SpaceX was unlikely to deploy all the satellites under the approval.
Opposition to space-based datacenters has also been raised in a report published earlier this month by Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy.

The paper, Space-Based Data Centers Roadmap: The Case for Caution, said that space-based datacenters were likely to become a reality before the risks of large-scale deployment can be fully understood or governed.

“To put even 10% of the artificial intelligence data centers anticipated by 2030 into orbit would require more than 700 launches of large rockets every year, about two per day, in perpetuity,” it said.

In a chapter titled “Night Sky and Astronomy”, the authors warned large satellite constellations “could cause a dramatic transformation of night skies around the world” as well as “large debris fields in low Earth orbit, loss of life and property damage from de-orbiting satellites, depletion of the stratospheric ozone layer and increased global warming”.
It added: “The current governance regimes will not be sufficient to manage these risks, especially as addressing many of the challenges will need to be coordinated on a global scale.”

title_en: Pummelling electronic trio Factory Floor’s first album in a decade shows signs of mellowing – but is it all a feint?
excerpt_en: One of the buzziest acts of the 2010s return with One Trip, which bathes their classic sound in a warmer light – until the buzzsaw synths and scattershot percussion explode
body_en: Devotees still speak in hushed awe about the intense, hypnotic performances by Factory Floor, one of the buzziest electronic groups of the 2010s. Even the band agree: Nik Colk Void (vocalist and modular synth wrangler) wistfully remembered them as “full of carnage” during their lengthy hiatus. So what on earth went down at Mutek Montreal in 2024? Their one-off reunion show proved so transformative that it inspired Factory Floor’s first album in 10 years.

Sounding uncharacteristically relaxed, opening single Continuation is a woozier take on their often grinding approach to repetition, building into blissful contentment rather than rabid euphoria. “It’s gonna be fun,” Void exhales. “It’s gonna be … easy.” This third album takes in Factory Floor’s favoured influences – brain-spinning industrial noise, eccentric acid techno, a Kraftwerkian clarity of purpose – and bathes them in a warmer light. But that’s not to say they’ve softened. Standout track Buzz Saw has the album’s toughest synth line, serrated and stomping, for what should be a new live classic.
Related: ‘On stage is the only time I can stop the worry’: Nik Colk Void on techno and letting go

With new percussionist Joe Ward joining Void and multi-instrumentalist Gabe Gurnsey, Factory Floor combine thumping, primal live drumming with programmed trickery and a raft of interesting textures. Druuuuum is a scattershot, heavily reverbed 22 seconds celebrating machine and human percussion, while Between You (recorded with New Order’s Stephen Morris) uses woodblock and tumbling hand drumming to raise the pulse. A strike pad for a new era of explosive (but perhaps slightly more holistic) shows, One Trip finds Factory Floor unable to resist what they do best.

title_en: Natural England objected to a datacentre. Weeks later ministers threatened to abolish the agency
excerpt_en: Body urged Bristol city council to reject plan because of risk to nearby protected wildlife and habitats
body_en: Natural England objected to the building of a large AI datacentre near Bristol weeks before the government threatened to abolish the independent environmental adviser.

The nature adviser made a significant intervention to urge Bristol city council not to grant planning permission for a 40MW datacentre at Avonmouth, because of the threat to protected wildlife and habitats at one of the UK’s most important sites for migratory birds, which is within 600 metres of the site.

The Environment Agency – which is also threatened with abolition by the de facto deputy prime minister, Louise Haigh – objected in addition to the flooding risk at the site, which is on a high-risk flood plain, expressing concerns people would not be able to take safe refuge in the event of a deluge.

Haigh this week blamed quangos, including Natural England, for blocking development and indicated both bodies could be scrapped with their responsibilities handed to ministers or devolved. Ministers are pushing for the construction of AI datacentres across the country as key to growing the UK economy.

Hundreds of AI datacentres are planned, with more than 300 waiting in the queue to connect to the electricity grid, representing 73GW of demand – almost double the peak winter energy demand for the entire UK. But they face considerable environmental and sustainability issues over their high energy use, pollution, encroachment on protected habitats and emissions from fossil fuel power stations many want to install while waiting for grid connections.

To side-step local democracy, the government is allowing datacentre developers to use the nationally significant infrastructure projects (NSIP) regime, with the secretary of state acting as the decision maker.
But Natural England has expressed concerns to ministers about the rollout of datacentres, urging caution and a precautionary approach.

In a response to the government’s draft datacentre national policy statement, Natural England said AI datacentres were a relatively new development type whose full environmental impacts were still being understood.
It highlighted the potential impact on rare and vulnerable species from overabstraction from waterways to meet datacentres’ demands.

Government sources denied the objection to the datacentre at Avonmouth or Natural England’s stance on taking a precautionary approach to their widespread construction had influenced Haigh’s announcement of their possible abolition.

But Craig Bennett, the chief executive of the Wildlife Trusts, said the government’s threatened abolition of Natural England was a worrying sign of an attack on environmental regulation. “Regulatory arm’s-length bodies like Natural England are set up to implement the law of parliament,” he said. “If we want decisions made about nature on the basis of science rather than the very last private corporate or vested interest that a minister has spoken to, then we have independent arm’s-length bodies like Natural England.”

Earlier this month Natural England advised Bristol city council that the datacentre could cause “disturbance and displacement” to rare and vulnerable bird species within the Severn estuary special protection area, just 600 metres away. Another protected site, Hallen Marsh, was only 270 metres away but had not been accounted for by the developers when assessing noise pollution, Natural England said.

As well as the flood risk, the Environment Agency said the developers had not provided any information on the level of water use, and the risk of pollution from land contamination to controlled waters. More than 4,000 people have objected to the datacentre’s construction.
Bristol council said the proposal was “likely to give rise to significant environmental effects” and it wanted the developers to carry out a full environmental impact assessment.

Mary Stevens, an AI campaigner at Friends of the Earth, said: “Natural England was doing its job brilliantly here as an independent adviser. I would have no confidence if this was a government minister doing the work because they would not be acting independently to protect nature.”

Rivington Energy, which is developing the datacentre, said: “We acknowledge the feedback received from the Environment Agency and Natural England and welcome the opportunity to continue working constructively with all consultees throughout the planning process.

“While substantial environmental and technical assessment work has already been undertaken, additional studies are being prepared in response to comments received and will be submitted as part of the ongoing planning process.
“We … are now preparing a detailed environmental statement to support the next stage of project assessment.”

The Wildlife Trusts have launched a petition to save Natural England, saying the current body and its predecessors have been vital protectors for wildlife, land, water and sea across England since the 1940s.

A government spokesperson said: “Datacentres are essential to our economy, but their development must protect the environment and benefit local communities. Developers must meet planning requirements, with local authorities assessing environmental impacts, and then deciding on local applications.”

title_en: Is Russia about to launch a nuclear weapon into Earth’s orbit? A space law expert explains the threat
excerpt_en: An agreement made nearly 60 years ago to keep nuclear weapons out of orbit could be put to the test.
body_en: Mikhail Svetlov/Getty Images As early as December. That’s how soon Russia could put a satellite carrying a nuclear weapon in orbit, according to German media reports.
If the news sounds familiar from headlines past, that’s because it is. In 2024, the United States made a similar allegation, albeit without giving any potential launch window.
These latest reports claim that the satellite, Sputnik-S, was assembled several years ago and is in storage near Moscow.

Intelligence agencies in NATO countries have reportedly shared information about the satellite. This week, the alliance’s secretary general asserted that protecting NATO territory includes keeping it safe from threats to space systems.

Russia’s embassy in Berlin said it “categorically reject[s] all these groundless allegations”. Echoing Moscow’s 2024 denial, it called the reports “propaganda”, adding that Russia “strictly adheres to the fundamental 1967 Outer Space Treaty”.
What is this treaty and what does it say about nuclear weapons? And how could the international community respond or even verify what is on board a satellite?
A lesson on cooperation The prospect of nuclear weapons off-Earth helped drive negotiations for the treaty invoked by Russia.

During the Cold War, the US and the Soviet Union found common ground on keeping these weapons out of orbit. It was a lesson on cooperation, despite competition and conflict, worth recalling in what is framed as today’s “space race”.
A cornerstone of international space law that prevails to this day, the Outer Space Treaty is also an arms control treaty. Under Article IV, countries undertake not to:

place in orbit around the Earth any objects carrying nuclear weapons or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction, install such weapons on celestial bodies, or station such weapons in outer space in any other manner.

Placing a nuclear weapon in orbit would itself breach the prohibition, even if it was never detonated. If a detonation did occur, it would breach the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty of 1963, which prohibits nuclear explosions in outer space and in the atmosphere.
Read more: Too many satellites? Earth’s orbit is on track for a catastrophe – but we can stop it
A nuclear ‘aurora’ No country is known to have ever placed a nuclear weapon in orbit. But there are examples from history of states detonating nuclear weapons off-Earth.

One summer’s night in 1962, people in Hawai'i gazed upward and saw what was, in effect, a nuclear “ aurora ”. One eyewitness, then a teenager, who was watching with her sibling from a spot overlooking Pearl Harbor, recalled the “exploding sky” and how it later turned “a deep blood red that lingered”.
The US had detonated a nuclear weapon about 400 kilometres above the Pacific Ocean in a classified test code-named Starfish Prime.
The US and the Soviet Union were testing nuclear weapons in space almost in lockstep, each demonstrating its advancing technological capabilities.
Starfish Prime was more than a visual spectacle. Of the 24 satellites in orbit at the time or launched in the following weeks, at least a third suffered damage.

The Starfish Prime ‘aurora’ seen from Honolulu. Capnez/Wikimedia What happens in space is a threat on Earth Today, the European Space Agency estimates there are about 15,800 functioning satellites in Earth’s orbit.

These satellites support the critical infrastructure we rely on every day, from navigation for transport to timing for banking and telecommunications. Whether we realise it or not, we are all “ space citizens ”.

Some satellites also support nuclear command, control and communications functions. Others give early warning of missile attacks. Researchers at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute examine this “space–nuclear nexus”.

During a conflict, leaders might interpret an attack on an early-warning satellite as “a precursor to a nuclear-first strike”. How they respond to that ambiguity could have escalatory risks and significance.
Mitigating the threat through verification So, what can the global community do to mitigate possible and actual threats of nuclear weapons in space?

title_en: Using AI to hunt for Black Friday bargains? That ‘great deal’ might not exist
excerpt_en: AI might be able to save you time researching Black Friday deals. But it can also hallucinate the answers.
body_en: The Conversation, CC BY-SA To get the most out of Black Friday sales, a bit of research is always useful. Ideally, this involves working out what you might want to buy – and checking prices – before sales begin.
Once the sales are under way, comparing prices, delivery costs and delivery times at different stores can feel onerous and time-consuming, especially if you’re worried you might miss out on a deal.
To streamline their search for a bargain, some shoppers are turning to artificial intelligence (AI) tools to do the research for them.
Can AI really help you snag a deal? The answer is yes, maybe. But there are reasons to proceed carefully.
Sending bots on a bargain hunt AI is being used to take the legwork out of all sorts of tasks. It makes sense consumers across the world are increasingly putting it to work as a shopping companion.

Say you’re looking for a new coffee machine or laptop this Black Friday. Rather than trawl through dozens of different sites yourself, you might ask a tool such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini to search the web for you and prepare a spreadsheet with a list of options.
A recent survey by the Australian Retail Council and market research firm Roy Morgan found this Black Friday, one in four respondents were planning to use an AI chatbot for research.
Among this group, 72% said it would be their first time doing so. If you fall into this category, there are a few things to be aware of as you check any recommendations.

Bogus bargains, ‘ghost stores’ and ads Hallucination is a well-known feature of generative AI tools. In the context of shopping with AI, this means some products, prices and stores may be entirely made up or misinterpreted.
A related concern is whether AI tools can reliably distinguish between genuine online stores and the fake or “ ghost stores ” that spring up online during sales periods.
Many AI tools, including the free and low-cost versions of OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google Search’s AI Overview and AI Mode, have already started rolling out advertising.
Both OpenAI and Google say advertisements shown to users are clearly labelled. But depending on your settings, the ads you see may be informed by your previous conversations with these tools.
Other generative AI tools don’t have ads. Anthropic, for example, has pledged to keep Claude ad-free. And Google’s Gemini app remains free of advertising, at least for now.

The other side of the checkout Even if you decide not to use AI this Black Friday, it could still shape the deals you see. Some retailers are reportedly already using AI to guide their discounting strategies.

AI is already changing the way companies decide what discounts to offer to everyone. Ashkan Forouzani/Unsplash This includes using sophisticated models and past sales data to work out the smallest discount they need to offer to sell a product.
Another potential headwind for shoppers is the use of AI by retailers to personalise prices to the amount a consumer is likely to be prepared to pay, sometimes called “ surveillance pricing ”.
Currently, this is not explicitly against the law unless the surveillance pricing involves discrimination based on protected characteristics such as race, sex or disability.
Read more: AI is using your data to set personalised prices online. It could seriously backfire

Handing over your wallet By Black Friday next year, new tools which go beyond simple research may be more commonplace: AI shopping agents. These tools can find stores selling what you’re looking for, compare prices and then complete the purchase on your behalf.
For example, Meta’s Muse agent, which launched in Australia last week, integrates with existing social media accounts and can complete tasks on your behalf.

Other tech companies are also venturing into the space. OpenAI recently launched its Dots agent, and Google’s offerings include Agentic Checkout and Gemini Tasks. Amazon offers its own shopping agent but blocks other third-party agents from accessing its site.
Can we make agents safe? Developers such as Meta say they are building in protections to prevent consumer AI agents “going rogue” and overstepping their authority or spending instructions.

title_en: 50 years of the Sex Pistols: not agents of chaos, but dreamers of a utopia
excerpt_en: The Sex Pistols are often thought to be obnoxious anarchists who promote chaos. But what if they were the opposite?
body_en: John Mead/Mirrorpix/Mirrorpix via Getty Images On November 26 1976, a London-based punk band released a record that created shock waves around the world.

While not the first punk single to be released (The Damned’s New Rose, Radio Birdman’s Burn my Eye EP, and I’m Stranded by the Saints were released a few weeks earlier), Anarchy in the UK, by the Sex Pistols set the tone and a high bar for what was to follow.
With its snarling lyrics (“I am an antichrist”) and raw sound, the song blew a gaping hole in 1970s complacency.
The Sex Pistols are often thought to be obnoxious anarchists who promoted chaos. But in many ways they were the opposite.
Here are five ways they created a template for a more inclusive, more tolerant, and better balanced society that remains relevant in today’s uncertain world.

1. Social and political convention Like many parts of the developed world, Britain in the mid-1970s faced economic decline, industrial unrest and growing disillusionment with established institutions.

Anarchy in the UK, followed by the band’s next single, God Save the Queen, released during Queen Elizabeth II’s Silver Jubilee in 1977, voiced the anger and alienation of many people while raising questions about national authority and identity.
The Pistols opened a door for many young people, inviting them to challenge established regimes, and to say no.
Their assertion that there was “ no future ” is also relevant today.
2. Style and fashion Alongside their strong influence on music, the Pistols heavily influenced style and fashion.

It is sometimes claimed the Pistols were conceived as a vehicle for Vivienne Westwood’s iconic clothing, which included bondage wear. As well as wearing her clothes, the band also took their name from her shop SEX on Chelsea’s Kings Road in London.
Westwood’s punk stylings encouraged others to create distinctive clothes and outfits from everyday and discarded items, including bin-bags and safety pins.

Sex Pistols manager Malcolm McLaren and Viviane Westwood outside Bow Street Magistrate Court, after being remanded on bail for fighting in 1977. Daily Mirror/Bill Kennedy/Mirrorpix/Mirrorpix via Getty Images Based on her work with the Sex Pistols, and their manager Malcolm McLaren, Westwood’s career as a fashion iconoclast continued until her death in 2022.

Elsewhere, graphic designer Jamie Reid ’s combination of “ransom note” typography and situationist style détournement has had a lasting effect on graphic art and design, while the filmic work of Julien Temple (who made the Sex Pistols 1980 film The Great Rock ‘n’ Roll Swindle) has heavily influenced the development of the rock biopic.
3. DIY One of the Pistols main influences was in the emergence of a DIY approach to music.

This is perhaps epitomised in the Pistols infamous gig at the Lesser Free Trade Hall in Manchester on June 4 1976, which inspired attendees to form their own bands (famously: Joy Division, Buzzcocks and The Smiths).

The Sex Pistols perform at the Lesser Free Trade Hall, Manchester, June 4 1976. Paul Welsh/Redferns via Getty Images. In this, the myth that the Pistols “couldn’t play” simply inspired the realisation that anyone could pick up a guitar and make a record.
This DIY approach also involved the dissemination and promotion of music and the artists, through home-made fanzines, the precursor to the blogs and zines that proliferate today.
4. Gender and inclusivity The Pistols encouraged women to become musicians.
Siouxsie Sioux was a member of the Pistols entourage, the Bromley Contingent, contributing to the chaos of the Sex Pistols’ infamous TV confrontation with Bill Grundy before founding the Banshees.

Palmolive and Viv Albertine of the Slits were previously members of the (unrecorded) Flowers of Romance along with John Ritchie (aka Sid Vicious). Chrissie Hynde, who had worked at SEX, went on to form The Pretenders. Poly Styrene was inspired to form X-Ray Spex having seen an early Pistols gig in Hastings in 1975.
The Pistols were central to a London punk scene that embraced and promoted diversity and difference at a time of racial tensions and intolerance.
